title: The Feel Stack: five layers of game sensation
body:
Game feel is not one property. It is five layers that a player experiences at once, and a screen can pass at one layer while failing at another. Diagnose the layer before changing values.

| Layer | Name | Core question |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Core game feel | Does input respond immediately, clearly, and consistently? |
| 2 | UI feel | Does touching the interface feel like playing the game? |
| 3 | Sensory juice | Is the meaning of the action amplified through sight, sound, touch, and time? |
| 4 | Experience arc | After the session ends, was it worth the time? |
| 5 | Engagement | Does the next action feel wanted rather than required? |

The ideal chain, in order: intent -> input -> immediate response -> clear state change -> sensory amplification -> meaning -> emotional reward -> next action. Every complaint about "feel" is one broken link in that chain.

| Broken link | What the player says | Where to look in Unity |
|---|---|---|
| input -> response | "I pressed it and nothing happened" | input polling site, Update vs FixedUpdate, animation lock-out state |
| response -> state change | "What changed?" | missing visual delta on the affected object or its UI mirror |
| state change -> amplification | "That felt flat" | no ParticleSystem, no AudioSource.PlayOneShot, no camera reaction |
| amplification -> meaning | "It is flashy but I do not care" | effect intensity does not track the value of the event |
| meaning -> next action | "Fine, but I am done" | no follow-up goal after the reward resolves |

Measure with both kinds of signal. Hard signals say what the build did: frame time, input-to-visible latency, lock-out duration, timing windows. Soft signals say what the player believed: weight, clarity, fairness, ownership. A build can be correct on every hard signal and still fail every soft one.

Separate the layers to analyse. Recombine them to decide: one button press travels through all five before the player forms an opinion.

Five principles, one per layer.
1. Input must be immediate. If input and output feel disconnected, the player stops feeling in control.
2. UI must feel like touchable objects. Buttons, cards, slots, bars, and popups are not flat images; they are objects the player handles.
3. Juice must amplify meaningful action. Amplifying meaningless actions produces noise, not satisfaction.
4. Experience is remembered at session scale. Players forget a single particle burst; they remember whether the session felt worthwhile.
5. Engagement should create desire, not pressure. The goal is a player glad to return, not one afraid to leave.

For the stack to hold, the core loop itself must qualify: predictable, immediate, easy to learn but deep to master, fresh across repetition, appealing even before rewards, organic in motion, and consistent with the game's chosen abstraction level. No amount of layering repairs a loop that fails these.

title: Four elements of core game feel
body:
Core game feel is the tactile satisfaction of controlling something. Four elements decide it, and they can be tuned independently.

| Element | Definition | Good state | Bad state |
|---|---|---|---|
| Responsiveness | Delay between input and visible reaction | The character leaves the ground on the frame the button is read | Motion starts 0.2-0.3s later with no readable reason |
| Weight | The sense that the object has mass | A heavy weapon starts slowly and settles slowly | Every object accelerates on the same curve |
| Impact | Strength of the collision or hit reaction | The target flinches, flashes, and displaces | The target absorbs the hit with no visible change |
| Consistency | Same input, same result | Jump apex is identical every time | Apex varies with frame rate or input timing |

Consistency is the one that is usually broken by accident rather than by design. In Unity the common causes are reading input in FixedUpdate (inputs land on physics ticks instead of frames), applying a force with Time.deltaTime inside FixedUpdate, or driving movement from an animation while also driving it from script.

Feel is the result the player judges. Juice is the set of tools that produce that judgement. Fixing a feel problem with more juice fails when the defect is at the input or state layer: amplification of an unclear event makes the event louder, not clearer.

title: The response loop and why amplification is not the source of fun
body:
The loop is: the game shows state, the player interprets it, the player acts, the game changes, and the change is shown back. Feel work lives almost entirely in the last step - how clearly and how quickly the change returns to the player.

Amplification is not the source of fun. Fun comes from a problem worth solving with the player's own judgement and hands. If the system is fully understood the moment it opens, no amount of effect work keeps it interesting. The pairing that works is a problem worth solving plus a response that lands hard.

Echo one action across several channels at once. The player fuses them into a single perceived event.

| Channel | Role | Unity site |
|---|---|---|
| Visual, target | change on the object that was acted on | material colour or emission flash, scale punch, displacement |
| Visual, world | the surroundings react | ParticleSystem burst, decal, camera reaction |
| Visual, UI | informational confirmation | damage number, bar change, icon pulse on the Canvas |
| Audio | emotional interpretation | AudioSource.PlayOneShot with pitch variation |
| Tactile | physical confirmation | gamepad rumble or Handheld.Vibrate on mobile |
| Time | perceptual emphasis | a few frames of Time.timeScale reduction |

Interrupt, do not blend, at the moment of impact. Kill the in-progress tween or coroutine on the target and start the reaction fresh. A 1-2 frame flash plus displacement that overrides current motion reads as a hit; the same reaction cross-faded into existing motion reads as mush. Insisting on smooth interpolation everywhere is the most common cause of soft-feeling impacts.

The loop closes only if the change carries consequence. A hit that cannot eventually kill, a fall that cannot fail, and a reward that changes nothing all break the last link no matter how well they are presented.

title: Latency budget, motion envelope, lock-out and cancel
body:
Control feel is the input side of game feel. It is decided before any presentation work, and presentation cannot repair it.

Latency budget. The human correction loop - see the screen, interpret, move the hand - runs at roughly 240ms, so the game has to answer well inside it.

| Case | Budget | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Any input to visible response | within 100ms | below this the response reads as continuous with the input |
| High-intensity action (attack, dodge, jump) | under 50ms | 3 frames at 60fps |
| UI button acknowledgement | 50-100ms | confirms receipt, separate from the result |
| Screen or mode transition | 200-500ms | gives time to re-read context |

The rule is not "make everything fast". It is to place delay deliberately: precision action gets none, a heavy attack earns startup and recovery, a strategy screen earns reading time.

Motion envelope. Shape the response instead of assigning it a single speed value.

| Element | Meaning | Effect on feel |
|---|---|---|
| Attack | time from input to full output | instant reads mechanical and precise; a short ramp reads organic and alive |
| Dimensionality | how many states the input carries | a button is on/off; a stick is direction plus magnitude |
| Sensitivity | output change per unit of input | high reads aggressive; low reads stable and heavy |
| Versatility | the space of expression made from combinations | where mastery and personal style live |

Applying acceleration and friction: snapping velocity to maximum on press and to zero on release feels mechanical. Interpolate toward a target speed each frame - for example `current = Mathf.MoveTowards(current, target, accel * Time.deltaTime)` - so mass appears without changing the maximum speed value. Shape deceleration deliberately against acceleration; symmetric reads neutral, slower deceleration reads heavy and slippery.

Lock-out and cancel. Whether a motion can be interrupted defines the character of the game.

| Structure | Trait | What it buys | What it costs |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lock-out | no control until the motion ends | commitment, weight, consequence | reads unfair if the window is not readable |
| Cancel | the motion can be interrupted into another action | responsiveness, skill ceiling | erases weight if permitted everywhere |
| Buffer | an early input is stored until it becomes valid | fewer dropped inputs | reads automatic if the window is long |
| Grace window | the action stays valid slightly past its normal window | fewer unfair failures | reads fake if visible |

Lock-out is not sloppiness. Combined with readable enemy patterns it is the source of tension, and the width and placement of the cancel window is what defines a specific game's hand. What makes lock-out feel unfair is not its length but its illegibility: the player must be able to see, before committing, that they are committing.

title: From device signal to game parameter
body:
The same button can feel direct, physical, authored, or systemic depending on what it changes and through what filter. Decide the whole chain, not just the key binding.

Read the device first. Hardware is not neutral - it defines what the hand can express before any code runs.

| Device lens | What to check | Design risk |
|---|---|---|
| Discrete or continuous | does the input carry momentary states or a continuous value | binary input driving fluid motion needs buffering, ramps, or explicit state |
| Dimensions and bounds | how many axes, and where motion stops | unbounded input feels precise but weightless; hard bounds feel stable but constrained |
| Signal shape | what raw values arrive over time | a sensitive device can still feel dull if the response curve is flat |
| Physical construction | travel, spring resistance, size of the contact area | the same mechanic feels different per device before a line of code changes |

Then decide what the input actually writes.

| Response lens | Options in Unity | Feel consequence |
|---|---|---|
| Mapping target | Transform position, rotation, Rigidbody force or linearVelocity, an Animator parameter, a spawned object, a simulation value | decides whether the action reads direct, physical, authored, or systemic |
| Reference frame | avatar-relative, camera-relative, world-relative, cursor-relative | a wrong frame makes correct input feel wrong when the view changes |
| Filtering | multipliers, AnimationCurve response curves, dead zones, smoothing | this is where raw input becomes tuned feel |
| State meaning | grounded, airborne, aiming, blocking, charging, stunned, menu focus | one input gains depth only if the state change is readable |
| Pattern reading | holds, chords, timed sequences, context-sensitive actions | expands expression, becomes noise if the rule is not predictable |

Preserve the separations that create the sensation. Collapsing them is the usual cause of stiff movement.

| Separation | What it protects | Failure if collapsed |
|---|---|---|
| Facing vs velocity | drift, carve, slide, thrust | motion snaps to a single stiff vector |
| Ground vs air response | state-readable mastery | one input behaves identically in incompatible states |
| Intended vs actual velocity | traction, slip, recovery | physics reads either fake or uncontrollable |
| Avatar frame vs camera frame | intuitive spatial control | correct input feels wrong after a camera cut |

Low device sensitivity can still feel expressive when the response has rich motion and clear states. High sensitivity can still feel empty when the response is only a position overwrite.

title: Space is the second tuning surface
body:
Response tuning does not stand alone. The same movement values feel empty in an open field, precise in a dense obstacle run, and unfair in a cramped collision layout. Tune motion and level together.

| Context layer | What it tunes | Failure it produces |
|---|---|---|
| Overall space | openness, enclosure, scale, travel distance | movement reads empty, or claustrophobic |
| Object spacing | density, obstacle size, avoidance rhythm | movement reads dull, or unfairly twitchy |
| Collision surface | friction, restitution, contact response, step height | objects read dead, slippery, sticky, or weightless |

Speed is relational. The absolute value on a movement component means little next to nearby object density, camera distance, field of view, surface texture, and the size of the thing being controlled. Doubling the speed value and doubling the corridor width can cancel out entirely.

Collision is relational too. The same collider reads solid, soft, sticky, or frictionless depending on how contact returns energy. In Unity the levers are the PhysicsMaterial friction and bounciness on the surface, the collider skin and step offset on the character, and whether contact is resolved by the physics solver or by an explicit script response.

Author the level against the movement envelope, not after it. Platform height, gap width, obstacle density, ramp angle, enemy speed, and camera room should all be derived from the tuned jump arc and top speed. A mechanic reads generous when the space gives its best motion room to breathe, and oppressive when the same values are forced through a layout that contradicts them.

Practical check: before changing a movement value because motion "feels wrong", measure the actual gap widths and obstacle spacing around the failure. The value is frequently correct and the space is not.

title: Forgiveness removes unfair failure, not difficulty
body:
Forgiveness is the system accepting normal human imprecision. It is not difficulty reduction, and it works only while it stays invisible.

| Technique | What it does | Failure it prevents | Typical window |
|---|---|---|---|
| Coyote time | jump stays valid briefly after leaving ground | falling after an edge that looked reachable | 0.08-0.15s |
| Jump buffer | a jump pressed before landing fires on landing | an input dropped for being slightly early | 0.10-0.20s |
| Action buffer | an attack or skill pressed during recovery fires when valid | broken chains during combos | 0.15-0.25s |
| Step assist | low ledges resolve automatically | snagging on pixel-scale corners | step height under the character radius |
| Ledge grab assist | near-miss ledge approaches are corrected | right intent, failed collision threshold | a small capsule around the hand target |
| Aim assist | targeting is nudged toward valid targets | stick and touch aiming instability | keep under a readable angle |
| Control lock budget | a cap on how long strong events remove control | a hit that reads as losing the controller | usually under 0.5s |

Implementation notes for Unity. Track the windows as timers advanced with Time.deltaTime and consumed on use, not as booleans. Keep the check in Update where input is read, so the window does not quantise to the physics tick. Grace windows must never be extended silently while the player holds a button; the window starts once per qualifying event.

Good forgiveness is invisible. The player should conclude "I did that correctly", never "the game helped me". If the assist is visible - a snap, a warp, a highlight - it converts mastery into charity.

Forgiveness cannot repair an ambiguous command. If one button sequence can produce two different high-impact actions with no readable state difference, the problem is command grammar and not difficulty. Resolve the overlap first; adding more grace to an ambiguous input makes the wrong action fire more reliably.

title: Representation, treatment, and the promise an object makes
body:
Every object makes a promise before it is touched. Its representation says what it is; its treatment says how literally it will behave. Feel breaks when the promise and the behaviour disagree.

| Lens | Question | Failure mode |
|---|---|---|
| Representation | what does this appear to be? | the player expects behaviour the system does not implement |
| Treatment | is the style realistic, iconic, or abstract? | visual fidelity promises a physical fidelity the game cannot support |
| Expected behaviour | how should it move, sound, collide, and break? | motion and effects contradict the object's promise |
| Abstraction match | do rules, visuals, audio, and interaction share one abstraction level? | the world reads inconsistent even when each asset is polished |

A more iconic treatment buys freedom. A more realistic treatment raises the debt owed in mass, traction, contact response, animation, and audio. A stylised vehicle can slide impossibly and stay believable; a photoreal one cannot.

When a mechanic is physically impossible, the treatment has to earn permission for it. Exaggerated jumps, frictionless slides, and improbable grapples read as correct inside an iconic world and as bugs inside a realistic one. Comedy loosens the standard but does not erase contradiction.

This is a practical check in Unity, not a stylistic one. When a hit reads wrong on a specific enemy, compare its silhouette and material against its actual mass, the impulse it receives, and the audio clip length. The mismatch is usually there rather than in the hit reaction itself. A large armoured shape given a light impulse and a thin impact sound reads broken no matter how well the effect is timed.

title: Session shape, need layers, and how a session should end
body:
Core feel is the moment of pressing. The experience arc is what the player remembers afterwards: how heavy it was to start, how fast the first goal appeared, how failure was handled, and whether stopping felt acceptable.

The shape of a healthy session: stable entry -> goal recognition -> core play -> rising tension -> resolution or failure -> recovery and reward -> preview of the next goal -> comfortable exit.

| Session length | Core goal | How to build it |
|---|---|---|
| 1 minute | immediate value | a check, a claim, a small cleanup |
| 5 minutes | one small completion | a single short loop closed |
| 15 minutes | meaningful progress | one mission, a partial chapter, one growth decision |
| 30 minutes | immersive play | several challenges, exploration, build testing |
| 1 hour or more | deep investment | long-term goals, social play, a major turn |

Every length needs closure. Short sessions close small, long sessions close deep, but a session that cannot close leaves the player feeling interrupted rather than finished.

Alternate the four attention states rather than holding one.

| State | Role | Design examples |
|---|---|---|
| Focused execution | control, reaction, decision | combat, puzzles, timing, strategy |
| Relaxed exploration | imagination, meaning, rest | wandering, appreciating, story, arranging |
| Salience switching | detecting that something now matters | warnings, rewards, enemy arrival, goal updates |
| Reward anticipation | expecting and receiving payoff | level up, discovery, acquisition, completion |

Sustained focus without release exhausts; sustained release without a goal bores; switches without warning startle; and payoff that never lands drains the anticipation state of meaning. After intense play the player needs release, and after long exploration the player needs a goal.

Player needs run in parallel, not in strict order.

| Layer | Need | Question |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Functional stability | is it stable, readable, and responsive? |
| 2 | Predictable safety | can the player understand rules and causes of failure? |
| 3 | Belonging | is there connection to a world, characters, or other players? |
| 4 | Mastery | does the player feel improvement and recognition? |
| 5 | Discovery | is curiosity and experimentation invited? |
| 6 | Aesthetic resonance | is inhabiting the game satisfying by itself? |
| 7 | Meaning | does anything remain after the session? |

A game can retain players through discovery or expression while higher layers are uneven, but a collapse at functional stability cannot be compensated for long.

Three-question test for any system: is the player choosing this voluntarily, does it produce a sense of growing skill, and does it connect them to a world or to other people? Two clear yes answers is a healthy system. One or none means the system is running on obligation.

Ending well. A good ending confirms saved progress, summarises what was accomplished, previews one next goal, and signals that stopping now is fine. A bad ending exaggerates loss on exit, stacks popups, and asks for decisions when the player is already tired.

Arc checklist:
- [ ] Is the first goal visible within the first 30 seconds?
- [ ] Can a short session still feel complete?
- [ ] Do long sessions carry both rising tension and release?
- [ ] After failure, is there a clear recovery path?
- [ ] After a reward, does the next goal appear naturally?
- [ ] Does ending the session leave satisfaction rather than pressure?
- [ ] Do focus and rest alternate?
- [ ] Does each system pass at least two of: voluntary choice, growing skill, connection?

title: Update, FixedUpdate, LateUpdate, and velocity layering
body:
Feel becomes muddy when input, simulation, and presentation share one update site. Unity already separates them; the discipline is to keep each responsibility where it belongs.

| Loop | Responsibility | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| Update | read input, run grace and buffer timers, decide intent | record intent here; do not accumulate physics here |
| FixedUpdate | movement, collision, forces, rules | deterministic and frame-rate independent; runs on the fixed timestep, not per frame |
| Animation and presentation | animation, particles, visual interpolation | must stay stable while frame rate varies |
| LateUpdate | camera follow, final visual offsets, cleanup | reads the settled state after everything else moved |

Two failures follow directly from mixing them. Reading input in FixedUpdate quantises the input to the physics tick, so the same press produces different results depending on when it lands. Moving the camera in Update makes it chase a target that has not finished moving, which reads as jitter.

Interpolation. A Rigidbody stepped on the fixed timestep is visually stuttery when rendered at a different rate. Rigidbody.interpolation accepts None, Interpolate, or Extrapolate; Interpolate on the player body removes the stutter that is otherwise mistaken for a performance problem. Rigidbody2D carries the same property. Set it on the objects the camera watches, not on everything - it costs a frame of position history per body.

Animator.updateMode decides which clock animation runs on: Normal for scaled game time, Fixed to align with the physics step, UnscaledTime to keep playing while Time.timeScale is reduced. UnscaledTime is what keeps UI and menu animation alive during a hit stop.

Velocity layering. Separate the movement the player asked for from the movement the world imposed.

| Layer | Meaning | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Intent velocity | produced by player control | walk, jump, dash |
| Impact velocity | produced by external events | knockback, landing rebound, explosion push |
| Presentation offset | visual only, no effect on collision | recoil kick, flinch, camera shake, UI jolt |

Without this separation, every increase in presentation strength damages control, because the visual offset and the simulated position are the same number. Keep the presentation offset on a child transform or on the camera, so the collider and the authoritative position never move for a purely visual reason. Merge two layers only as a deliberate feel decision, never as an implementation shortcut.

Frame-rate safety. Time.deltaTime is clamped by Time.maximumDeltaTime, so a hitch cannot produce one enormous step - useful to know before compensating for it manually. When comparing feel between machines, pin Application.targetFrameRate and check whether the difference survives.

title: Juice: maximum output for minimum input
body:
Juice is the feedback layer that returns the largest possible response for the smallest possible input. One button press produces change across sight, sound, touch, and time, and the player concludes that their action genuinely affected the world.

Juice is the method; feel is the result. Feel is the player's final judgement that a game is good to control. Juice is the collection of tools - easing, deformation, particles, camera reaction, freeze frames, audio, haptics - used to produce that judgement.

The defining constraint: juice changes perception without changing the simulation. If an effect can be removed and the rules still work, it is presentation. If removing it changes collision, movement, damage, or progression, it is no longer juice and it belongs in the systems layer, where it needs tests rather than taste.

Three properties follow from that constraint.
- The effect is cumulative. Any single element is trivial on its own; twenty small ones applied to the same event change the perceived quality of the build entirely. This is also why a juice pass is hard to evaluate one commit at a time.
- Its absence is felt but not diagnosed. Players report that a build is bland, cheap, or unresponsive without being able to name what is missing, because nothing is missing from the rules.
- It is independent of art quality. Simple art with strong response reads as finished; expensive art without it reads as though something is broken.

What juice cannot do: create meaning that the action does not have. Amplifying an event that carries no consequence produces noise, and the player learns to ignore the channel. The pairing that works is a meaningful action plus precise amplification, in that order.

title: Tweening and easing
body:
Tweening computes the intermediate values between two states. Easing decides whether that transition accelerates, decelerates, or overshoots. Nothing in the physical world moves at a constant rate, so linear motion reads mechanical and cheap.

The one-line ease-out. Run per frame to move a value a fixed fraction toward its target:

x += (target - x) * 0.1f;

That single line produces natural deceleration - fast at first, slowing near the target - with no tween library. It is frame-rate dependent by construction, so for anything that must match across machines use `Mathf.Lerp(x, target, 1f - Mathf.Exp(-k * Time.deltaTime))` or drive the value from an AnimationCurve sampled over an explicit duration.

| Easing | Motion | Use for | How often |
|---|---|---|---|
| Linear | constant rate | almost nothing | rare |
| EaseOut | fast then settling | arrival, landing, UI entrance | constant |
| EaseIn | slow then accelerating | exits, charge-up, suction | frequent |
| EaseInOut | smooth both ends | screen and menu transitions | frequent |
| Back | slight overshoot then return | popups, buttons, acquisition | frequent |
| Bounce | rebound on arrival | playful rewards | occasional |
| Elastic | wobble on arrival | alerts, special rewards | sparing |

Reference values.
- Button hover: 100% -> 110%, EaseOut, 0.15s.
- Popup entrance: scale 0 -> 100% with Back overshoot around 0.3, 0.3s.
- Staggered entrance: 0.03-0.05s between elements; 20 elements land in 0.6-1.0s total.

Stagger is what separates a considered screen from a synchronised one. Elements arriving on the same frame read as a single sheet; a small offset per element reads as a composed layout.

In Unity these curves can come from an AnimationCurve field, from an Animator state, or from a tween package if the project already carries one. Use whatever the project already has - the curve shape matters, the library does not.

title: Squash and stretch
body:
Deformation is how an object declares its material and mass. A hard object barely deforms; a soft one deforms a lot. Volume reads as conserved: squash vertically and it widens, stretch vertically and it narrows.

| Style | X | Y | Fits |
|---|---|---|---|
| Realistic | 90-110% | 110-90% | simulation, sports |
| Cartoon | 70-130% | 130-70% | casual, platformer |
| Exaggerated | 50-150% | 150-50% | comic, party |

Impact sequence: round (100/100) -> flattened on contact (130/70) for 0.02s -> elongated on release (80/120) for 0.05s -> settle to (100/100) with EaseOut over 0.1s.

Button press: default (100/100) -> pressed (105/95) over 0.05s -> released (95/105) over 0.05s -> settle with EaseOut over 0.1s.

Character locomotion, where the value is highest: crouch before takeoff (110/90) for 0.05s, stretch while rising (90/110) scaled by vertical speed, round at the apex, compress hard on landing (120/80) for 0.05s, settle with EaseOut or a slight Back over 0.1-0.15s. None of the movement data changes; the springiness is entirely staging.

Deform the visual, never the collider. Scale a child renderer transform, or drive the shader, and leave the collider at its authored size. Scaling the GameObject that owns the collider changes collision behaviour and hit registration, which turns a presentation change into a gameplay bug.

Dash staging, without touching the speed value: stretch along the travel direction (roughly 150/70) with an EaseOut return; 3-5 fading silhouettes at 0.1-0.2s intervals or a trail; a short 0.02-0.03s freeze at the start frame for the snap.

Enemy hits use the same tool - flatten sideways to about (130/70) and return, and a static sprite reads as something living.

title: Particle systems
body:
Particles are the residue of an action. They are what proves the action touched the world rather than only the target.

Use the built-in ParticleSystem, or VFX Graph when the project already uses it and the counts are high. Building a custom particle engine is the classic way to spend a month and ship nothing; the built-in system covers every case below.

| Type | Use | Count and lifetime |
|---|---|---|
| Impact | hits, wall contact, destruction | 5-10 light, 20-50 heavy; 0.3-0.8s |
| Trail | movement, dash, projectiles | length scales with speed; opacity 1 -> 0 |
| Ambient | mood and depth | continuous, low density, never blocks reading |
| Reward | pickups, growth, completion | scaled to actual value, see below |
| Destruction | debris and fragments | fragments at 10-30% of the source size, with gravity and rotation |

Direction carries meaning: impact particles emit against the contact normal, trails emit behind travel, destruction debris inherits the impulse. A radial burst on every event flattens all of them into the same event.

Reward scaling, which must track real value rather than excitement: common gets a 3-5 particle sparkle; rare gets a 10-20 particle burst with a light camera reaction; top tier gets a 30-50 particle burst with a strong camera reaction and a dedicated sound.

Performance and cleanup. Pool systems instead of instantiating per event, cap the emission count on mobile, and keep Stop Action set so finished systems return to the pool rather than accumulating in the scene. Ambient systems are the usual source of a slow leak in a long session, because nothing ever ends them.

More particles is not better. Direction, lifetime, colour, and timing have to agree with the action's meaning, and a burst that outlives the action it describes reads as a bug.

title: Screen shake
body:
Shake converts impact into visual motion. The brain reads a shaking view as physical shock, which is why an otherwise flat hit lands the moment shake is added, and why an over-shaken game becomes unreadable.

| Parameter | Light | Medium | Strong |
|---|---|---|---|
| Amplitude | 2-5px | 5-15px | 15-30px |
| Duration | 0.05-0.1s | 0.1-0.3s | 0.3-0.5s |
| Frequency | 30-60Hz | 30-60Hz | 30-60Hz |
| Decay | exponential | exponential | exponential |

Rules that keep it usable.
- Randomise direction across 360 degrees. Pure horizontal shake reads as a glitch.
- Decay is mandatory. Constant-amplitude shake reads mechanical.
- Sum concurrent shakes but clamp the total, around 40px, or a crowded fight becomes unreadable.
- Reduce to 70-80% on handheld screens; the same pixel displacement is a larger fraction of a small view.
- Ship an intensity slider and an off option. This is an accessibility requirement, not a preference: strong view motion causes real nausea, and the developer is the least reliable judge because they adapted to it during development.

Implementation. Apply shake as a presentation offset on the camera, not on the authoritative transform: offset a child of the camera, or add the displacement in LateUpdate after follow logic has settled. Shake that writes the camera's real position fights the follow rig and drifts. Scale the whole system through one multiplier so the accessibility setting is a single value, and clamp it so a value of zero is genuinely zero.

Every genre benefits from some amount, including puzzle and card games - a 2px, 0.05s tick on a placement is felt without being seen.

title: Hit stop and freeze frames
body:
A very short pause at the moment of impact gives the brain time to register what happened. It is the cheapest way to make a hit read as heavy, and the easiest to overuse.

| Situation | Freeze |
|---|---|
| Light hit | none, or 0.01-0.02s |
| Normal hit | 0.02-0.04s (1-2 frames at 60fps) |
| Heavy hit or critical | 0.05-0.1s (3-6 frames) |
| Finisher | a longer freeze followed by slow motion |

It applies outside combat too: a few frames at the start of a dash or on a hard landing separate the input from its result and sharpen both.

Implementation in Unity. Reduce Time.timeScale toward zero and restore it after an unscaled delay - `WaitForSecondsRealtime` in a coroutine, or a timer advanced with Time.unscaledDeltaTime. Three details decide whether it reads as intentional or as a stall:
- Keep UI and menu animation running by driving them from unscaled time; an Animator set to UnscaledTime update mode continues through the freeze.
- Buffer input during the freeze and release it immediately after, or the pause eats the player's next command.
- Never reduce timeScale for longer than the input buffer window; past that the player feels the loss of control rather than the impact.

Longer is not stronger. Stacked hit stops during rapid attacks read as frame drops, so cap the total contribution per second and skip the freeze entirely on light repeating hits.

title: Knockback
body:
Knockback converts force into distance and direction. It tells the player how hard the hit was, where it came from, and how the fight just changed shape.

| Element | Standard |
|---|---|
| Direction | opposite the contact point or along the attack vector |
| Distance | scales with attack strength, target mass, and defensive state |
| Duration | short and readable; 0.1s normal, 0.15s heavy, 0.2-0.3s explosive |
| Decay | strong at first, settling quickly, EaseOut |
| Collision | the presentation and the gameplay collision must not disagree |

Reference distances in world units: 0.3-0.5 for a normal hit, 1.0-2.0 for a heavy hit, 3.0-5.0 for an explosion.

Scale by mass rather than applying a constant. A heavy enemy that slides the same distance as a light one erases both of their identities. Heavy targets should take an upper-body reaction, a short foot slide, and a camera response instead of displacement.

Self-knockback is where knockback becomes a mechanic instead of an effect. If firing pushes the player back, the fire button acquires a cost, and the player has to decide when not to press it. That single change converts recoil from decoration into a movement tool - firing downward extends hang time, firing while running slows the advance - and it is juice and gameplay at the same time.

Knockback applied to the player removes agency, so it needs a budget. Keep the control-loss window under the input buffer length, and keep it consistent, or every hit reads as a disconnected controller.

title: Camera feel
body:
The camera is part of the control scheme, not a viewer. A camera that lags, overreacts, or looks in the wrong direction makes correct input feel wrong.

| Technique | Purpose | Reference values |
|---|---|---|
| Damped follow | smooth pursuit | interpolation factor 0.1-0.3; below 0.05 the camera loses the target |
| Dead zone | ignores small target motion | sized so idle bob and small steps do not move the view |
| Look ahead | shows where the player is going | offset of speed x 0.5-1.0 units, EaseOut over about 0.3s |
| Camera kick | recoil and impact feedback | 3-10px against the action, EaseOut return over 0.1s |
| Zoom | emphasis on a moment | 1.0 -> 1.2 for a finisher over 0.2s; 1.0 -> 0.9 on an explosion over 0.3s |
| Speed-reactive FOV | amplifies velocity | 60 to 70-80 degrees at top speed in 3D; 1.0 to 0.9-0.95 orthographic size in 2D |

Look ahead is the difference between a camera that follows the player and one that serves the game. If the play happens ahead of the avatar - shooting, driving, running - show more of ahead. The same principle extends to threats: biasing the view slightly toward the centroid of incoming projectiles lets the player react to things that would otherwise be off screen.

Dead zones are control tuning, not polish. Follow every motion and the view reads seasick; follow too late and the avatar reads detached. Change the dead zone by state - a tight zone while aiming, a loose one while running, a taller one while jumping - because the visual stability each state needs is different.

Speed-reactive FOV has to be smoothed or it induces nausea: interpolate the FOV value itself at 0.05-0.1 per frame, widen faster than it narrows, and clamp the total swing. Half the sensation of speed in racing and running games comes from this one value; the same actual speed reads dramatically faster through a widening view.

Implementation. Run follow, look ahead, and damping in LateUpdate so the camera reads a settled target position. Keep shake and kick as offsets applied after the follow result, never written into the follow target. If the project uses the optional virtual-camera package, the same values live on its damping, dead-zone, and lens settings, and the shake stays a separate impulse layer.

Strong view motion and FOV swings require an intensity option, for the same reason screen shake does.

title: Sound design
body:
Sound is the fastest channel the player has for interpreting a result. A change in sound is perceived as a change in the quality of the game itself, which is why audio work returns more per hour than almost any other feel work.

Principles.
- Give every interaction a sound. Silence reads as a missing response, not as restraint.
- Match tone to meaning: bright and rising for gain, low and short for failure, a rising line for anticipation resolving into reward.
- Reinforce the low end on impacts. Adding sub-bass around 60-100Hz to hit and explosion sounds is the difference between a weapon that reads weak and the same weapon reading powerful, with no gameplay change at all.
- Separate the three contact sounds: the impact transient, the sustained motion loop, and the surface scrape. Each explains a different kind of contact, and collapsing them makes every surface feel identical.
- Scale pitch, weight, and duration by object size, impact strength, and reward value, so the ear hears the same hierarchy the eye sees.
- Synchronise animation playback with actual movement speed. Visible foot slip separates the character from the simulation faster than any audio defect.

Repetition control. Limit simultaneous copies of one clip to 3-5 voices, and vary AudioSource.pitch by plus or minus 5-8% per instance to avoid the machine-gun effect. Use AudioSource.priority so a critical sound is never stolen by ambient clutter, and route categories through an AudioMixer so an accessibility or comfort setting can attenuate one group without silencing feedback.

Rising pitch for escalation is a different tool from random pitch and must not be mixed with it. Randomisation removes repetition fatigue; a deliberate pitch ladder across a combo, a coin chain, or a score tally creates mounting tension. Their purposes are opposite, so a chain that also randomises loses the ladder.

title: Haptics
body:
Haptics is the feedback channel that reaches the hand. It is the least used and among the most effective, because it adds a third channel without adding screen clutter or audio load.

| Situation | Pattern | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Button confirmation | single light tap | 5-10ms |
| Common pickup | single light tap | 10-20ms |
| Successful hit | single medium pulse | 20-30ms |
| Critical hit | strong pulse, gap, weak pulse | around 50ms |
| Charge complete | rising intensity | around 200ms |
| Error or failure | quick double tap | 30ms twice |
| Top reward or finisher | patterned sequence | 80-120ms |

Platform reality in Unity. Handheld.Vibrate exists in UnityEngine and triggers a crude full-device buzz with no duration or intensity control, which is adequate for a failure or a rare event and too blunt for per-hit feedback. Fine-grained patterns and controller rumble come from the optional input package or a platform plugin, so treat detailed haptics as an optional layer and never as the only carrier of information.

Rules. Repeated haptics fatigue the hand and drain the battery, so reserve them for events that matter. Always ship an intensity and off option. Never convey state through vibration alone; it is a reinforcement channel for something already visible or audible.

title: Permanence
body:
Permanence is the evidence that the player passed through. Debris, shells, marks, fallen enemies, and cleared space all say the same thing: this world registered what I did.

What to leave behind.
- Fallen enemies that hold for 2-3 seconds before fading, or remain for the level when the budget allows.
- A physics collapse in the direction of the hit, using the knockback impulse as the death impulse, so the weight of the blow carries into the death.
- A dissolve fallback where a physics body is too expensive; nothing remains, but the certainty of the kill is preserved.
- Spent shells, fragments, impact decals on walls, and destructible background objects that do not affect play but do record the fight.
- Visible cleanup of a cleared area, so returning through it reads differently from entering it.

The payoff is spatial memory. A corridor the player fought through should be recognisable on the way back, and that recognition is what converts a level from a sequence of encounters into a place.

Budget in Unity. Pool the remains and cap the live count at 50-100, retiring the oldest first. Disable colliders and rigidbodies on settled remains and keep only the renderer, since the cost is usually in the physics rather than the drawing. Simplify or cull distant remains. Distinguish the traces that carry meaning from decorative residue: past a certain density, clutter starts hiding the things the player needs to read.

title: Personality
body:
Objects, enemies, buttons, and menus need character, not only correct function. The cost is small and the return is disproportionate, because personality is what makes a player care about an object before it has done anything.

Methods.
- Gaze. Give an object eyes that track what matters - the ball, the nearest enemy, the cursor - with a gaze interpolation of 0.1-0.2. Adding eyes to an abstract shape produces an emotional connection out of proportion to the work. Blinking is a brief renderer toggle.
- Situational expression. A worried face while threatened, a pleased one on success, a bored one while idle.
- Idle life. Breathing at 100% to 101-102% on a 2-3 second EaseInOut cycle; a distinct idle variation after a period of no input.
- Barks. A short line in the moment - on being hit, on a reward, while waiting. Pull from a pool at random with a cooldown so lines never repeat back to back, pop the bubble in with a small Back scale, hold 2-3 seconds, then fade. Text alone buys a large amount of personality for very little cost.

Reactions of this kind belong on presentation transforms and renderers, so an idle breathing scale never touches a collider or a layout that other systems measure.

Constraints. Personality must not cost control clarity, and UI personality must never outrank information delivery. The same function can carry a different tone per game, but a button that entertains while obscuring its state is a defect.

title: Dynamic lighting
body:
If particles convey quantity, light conveys energy. The same muzzle flash reads completely differently as a flat sprite versus a light that actually illuminates the wall, the floor, and the character.

Techniques.
- Momentary point light at the moment of firing or impact - a Light enabled for 0.05-0.1s with its intensity decaying on EaseOut. Enabling and disabling an existing light is far cheaper than instantiating one.
- Full-screen flash for decisive events only: 1-2 frames, 0.03-0.05s, white or the action's colour, returning immediately.
- Emissive projectiles and hazards contributing as real light sources, so a passing shot briefly tints the surfaces it travels past.

| Situation | Intensity and duration |
|---|---|
| Normal shot halo | small radius, 0.05s |
| Heavy hit or skill | medium radius with colour tint, 0.1s |
| Explosion or finisher | full-screen flash, 0.03-0.05s |

Light has to track real importance. When everything glows, glow stops meaning anything, and the player loses the cue that separates a threat from decoration.

Accessibility and cost. Repeated bright flashes carry a photosensitivity risk, so cap frequency and intensity and provide a flash-reduction option alongside the motion options. Real-time lights and shadows are expensive; on constrained hardware limit the light count, disable shadows on effect lights, or substitute an additive sprite glow, which reads nearly the same in motion. Never carry information by light colour alone.

title: Layering one event across channels
body:
The player does not perceive six effects. They perceive one event, assembled from whatever arrived within the same short window. Judge the assembled result, not the assets in isolation.

A worked hierarchy for a hit event:

| Grade | Visual | Audio | Tactile | Time |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Light | flash 0.05s, 5 particles | mid-range impact | 10ms | none |
| Medium | flash, knockback, 20 particles | impact with reinforced low end | 30ms | 0.05s freeze |
| Heavy | flash, knockback, 10px shake, 40 particles | dedicated critical layer | 50ms | 0.1s freeze |
| Decisive | full-screen effect, zoom, 20px shake | dedicated finisher line | 100ms pattern | 0.15s freeze plus slow motion |

Coherence beats budget. A small set of cues that agree - animation timing, audio pitch, debris scale, displacement distance - describes one mass and one material convincingly. An expensive set that disagrees describes five different realities and reads as noise, which is the usual reason a heavily worked effect still feels wrong.

Timing is the part that breaks first. Everything meant to be one event has to land inside roughly 50ms; audio arriving two frames after the visual is perceived as a separate, weaker event. Check the timing before adding another layer.

title: Making mass, material, friction, and force legible
body:
Most feel complaints are really complaints about a property the player cannot read. Decide which property the effect is supposed to communicate, then choose cues that all point at it.

| Property | Cues that build it | What breaks it |
|---|---|---|
| Mass | slower follow-through, longer settle, deeper audio, heavier dust, restrained displacement | a large object that accelerates instantly reads light regardless of its size |
| Material | impact tone, fragment shape, deformation amount, particle texture | one generic impact effect makes stone, metal, and flesh identical |
| Friction | skid marks, scrape loops, resistance in motion, surface-specific debris | frictionless glancing contact makes solid objects feel oily |
| Force | hit stop, recoil, camera kick, sharp directional burst | stacked force cues that disagree become noise |

In Unity the physical half of these is checkable rather than guessable: Rigidbody mass and drag, the PhysicsMaterial friction and bounciness on the surface, the impulse actually applied, and the length of the audio transient. When a hit reads wrong, compare those numbers against the object's apparent size and material before touching the effect.

Presentation must not change the simulation. If an effect can be removed and the rules still work, it is polish; if removing it changes collision, movement, damage, or progression, it is no longer polish and it belongs in the systems layer where it can be tested.

title: The intensity ladder
body:
If every event is presented at the same strength, nothing is special and the player stops reading intensity as information.

| Grade | Strength | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Micro | 1 | button, toggle, minor pickup |
| Minor | 2 | normal hit, small reward |
| Major | 3 | level up, heavy hit, objective complete |
| Epic | 4 | boss defeated, rare reward |
| Decisive | 5 | ending, top-tier reward, long-term goal |

The rule is one line: do not present a grade-2 event at grade-5 strength. Over-presentation of small events costs twice - it spends the vocabulary needed for the real peaks, and it teaches the player that presentation does not predict value.

The ladder also governs the screen. Reward and celebration screens can carry exaggeration freely, while precision screens - forms, drag interactions, competitive HUDs - need restraint, because motion there costs accuracy. The same effect can be correct on one screen and wrong on the next, so the question is always what this screen asks the player to do.

Grade the events in a spreadsheet before implementing them. Assigning intensity per event after each is built is how a project ends up with five different grade-5 presentations and no grade-1.

title: Button feedback: the five states
body:
The button is the smallest unit of interaction and the most repeated. If buttons feel dead, the whole game feels dead, whatever happens in play.

States: Normal -> Hover or focus -> Press -> Release -> Normal, with Disabled reachable from any of them.

| State | Specification |
|---|---|
| Normal | default colour and 100% scale; optional idle breathing 100% to 101% on a 2s cycle |
| Hover or focus | 110% scale, EaseOut, 0.15s, roughly 5% brighter |
| Press | 110% -> 95%, EaseOut, 0.05s, roughly 10% darker - this one must be immediate |
| Release | 95% -> 110% -> 100% with Back, 0.2s, click sound, 5-10ms haptic |
| Disabled | desaturated, 60-70% opacity, interaction blocked, reason shown if the block is not obvious |

Unity implementation. Selectable.transition accepts None, ColorTint, SpriteSwap, or Animation. ColorTint alone cannot produce the scale punch above, so drive scale from script or from an Animator on the Animation transition. Keep the scale on the button's RectTransform child rather than on a transform that a LayoutGroup controls, or the layout will fight the animation every frame. Use a CanvasGroup for the disabled state so opacity and raycast blocking change together.

Touch. There is no hover state on a touchscreen, which makes press feedback the only acknowledgement the player gets, so it must be instant. Keep the touch target at 44x44pt or 48x48dp minimum regardless of the visual size - expand the raycast area rather than the artwork - and space destructive buttons away from routine ones. Respect Screen.safeArea so nothing lands under a notch or a gesture bar.

title: Popups and modals
body:
A popup has to take attention without breaking flow. The asymmetry between entering and leaving is the whole technique.

| Stage | Specification |
|---|---|
| Enter | scale 0 -> 100% and fade 0 -> 100%, Back with about 0.3 overshoot, 0.25-0.35s |
| Background | 40-60% dim, fading in over 0.2s, blocking interaction behind |
| Hold | one core message and clearly separated options |
| Exit | scale 100% -> 80% with fade out, EaseIn, 0.15-0.25s |

Entrances should be readable and expressive; exits should be quiet and fast. A slow exit reads as the game arguing with the decision that was just made.

Unity implementation. Block the background with a full-screen Graphic that has raycastTarget enabled rather than by disabling other components, and drive the whole panel through one CanvasGroup so alpha, interactable, and blocksRaycasts move together. Popups that appear during a hit stop or slow motion need their animation on unscaled time, or they will crawl.

Popup fatigue is a real cost and needs structural control: never re-expose the same offer in one session, apply a cooldown after a dismissal, make "do not show again" genuinely work, queue by importance instead of stacking, and keep forced interruptions out of active play.

title: Number changes, damage numbers, criticals
body:
An instant number change is accurate and unfelt. The player reads the new value without perceiving the size of the change, which is the part that matters.

Count-up. Step from the old value to the new over 0.2-0.4s with EaseOut, stepping about every 0.05s. Punch the label to 120% and back for a large gain. For a chain - combos, coin runs, score tallies - raise the tick pitch progressively so the ear tracks the run; that ladder is a different tool from the random pitch used to avoid repetition, and mixing them destroys it.

Damage numbers. Enter with scale 0 -> 120% -> 100% over 0.15s, drift upward about 50px over 0.5s, fade during the last 0.2s. Colour by meaning, not by decoration: one colour for normal, a distinct one for critical. Offset concurrent numbers so they never overlap into an unreadable pile.

Critical presentation: start at 150% instead of 120%, add a 10px 0.1s camera reaction, a dedicated audio layer, an outline or glow, and a stronger haptic pulse around 50ms.

Unity implementation. Pool the damage-number objects; instantiating one per hit is the standard cause of a mid-fight hitch. Prefer a single pooled world-space Canvas for them over one Canvas per number, since every Canvas is a separate rebuild. TextMeshPro handles the outline and glow without a second object.

title: Health and progress bars
body:
A bar is a tension device, not a readout. The technique is to separate what the value is from how it got there.

Dual-response damage. On taking damage the front bar moves to the new value immediately or within 0.1s with EaseOut, while a trailing chip bar behind it catches up over about 0.4s with EaseOut. The gap between them is the size of the hit, expressed as distance and time. Flash the border for 0.1s at the moment of the change.

Increase. Fill over 0.2-0.3s with EaseOut, flash once at the start of the increase so the gain is noticed, and add a particle build before a fill completes with a light burst and a ready sound at completion.

Segmented bars. When the value should be felt rather than read, split it into cells: pop each cell as it changes, stagger multiple changes by 0.03-0.05s so they tick in sequence, and keep filled and empty cells in strong contrast.

Low health. Below 25%, add a red pulse, desaturation, a warning sound, and a 1-2px tremor, with the pulse rate rising as the value falls. Never carry that state on colour alone - the pulse and the tremor are what make it readable to a colour-blind player.

Unity implementation. Use Image with type Filled for the fill so no layout rebuild occurs per frame; animating width or anchors instead forces a Canvas rebuild on every update. Keep both bars on the same Canvas, and put frequently animated UI on its own Canvas so its rebuilds do not dirty static elements.

title: Notifications and toasts
body:
Enter by sliding in with EaseOut over 0.3s, hold 2-5 seconds depending on length, and exit by sliding or fading with EaseIn over 0.2s. Notifications the player must act on stay until they are dismissed.

Queue by importance. High-priority messages display immediately and displace the rest; low-priority ones queue and play in sequence; repeats of one type collapse into a count rather than stacking. Three simultaneous toasts communicate less than one.

The tone rule matters more than the timing. A notification is information or an invitation. The moment it works by implying loss - what will disappear, what is being missed, who noticed the absence - it converts a feedback channel into pressure, and players learn to dismiss the channel entirely.

Unity implementation. Pool toast objects and drive them from one queue owner rather than instantiating per event, and give the container its own Canvas so an incoming toast does not rebuild the HUD.

title: Inventory, acquisition, and rarity
body:
Acquisition and equipping look minor and are repeated more than almost anything else, which makes them a large share of perceived quality.

Acquisition sequence: the item travels toward the player or the target slot over about 0.3s with EaseIn and a trail, the destination slot glows and punches 100% -> 120% -> 100% over about 0.5s, the acquisition sound plays, and a short notification confirms it.

Rarity has to track actual value, since this is where presentation honesty is tested most often.

| Tier | Visual | Camera | Audio | Haptic |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Common | default, small sparkle | none | default pickup | 10ms |
| Uncommon | coloured glow | none | pickup with a rising tail | 20ms |
| Rare | glow and particles | 3px, 0.1s | dedicated pickup | 30ms |
| Epic | light burst | 5px, 0.15s | dramatic line | 50ms |
| Legendary | full burst with streaks | 10px, 0.2s | fanfare | 100ms pattern |

Equipping: highlight the slot, move the item into it, update the preview and the stats immediately, animate the stat delta as a count-up, and confirm with sound. Unequipping deserves its own feedback - a change the player made that produces no response reads as a failed input.

If a low-value result receives high-tier presentation, the tier vocabulary stops predicting anything and the player stops trusting the screen.

title: Screen transitions
body:
Every transition needs an animation. An instant cut triggers an orienting response and reads as a glitch, and the cost of avoiding it is a fraction of a second.

| Transition | Technique | Duration | Easing |
|---|---|---|---|
| Between peers | slide left or right | 0.3s | EaseInOut |
| Parent to child | slide up, or scale in | 0.3s | EaseOut |
| Child to parent | slide down, or scale out | 0.25s | EaseIn |
| Scene change | fade through black | 0.5-1.0s | EaseInOut |
| Entering combat | a distinct dedicated transition | 0.5-1.5s | authored |

Direction should encode structure: going deeper and coming back out must not look the same, or the player loses their place in the hierarchy.

Buffer the emotional transitions as well as the visual ones. Combat ending straight into an exploration screen gives no space to register the result; 2-3 seconds of resolution - the outcome, then the reward, then the return - is what makes the change feel finished rather than interrupted.

Unity implementation. Cover an additive or async scene load with the fade rather than freezing on the last frame, and keep the transition Canvas on its own sorting layer so nothing draws over it mid-change.

title: Microinteractions
body:
A microinteraction is the small response attached to a single act: a toggle flipping, a refresh spinning, a like bursting, a progress bar completing. Each carries information, confirms the act, and offers a small reward.

| Interaction | Information | Reward |
|---|---|---|
| Toggle flip | state changed | a physical click, squash and stretch plus sound |
| Refresh or load | the system is working | the wait becomes watchable |
| Confirm burst | the action registered | a small particle and audio payoff |
| Progress completion | the task is finished | light burst and a completion tone |

The test is whether it is felt without being noticed. If the player consciously admires the animation, it is already too long or too large. Half of the work is deletion.

Deliberate delay is a legitimate tool. A 0.2-0.5s acknowledgement with a progress animation on saving or equipping makes the change feel committed, where an instantaneous result on an important action can read as though nothing happened.

title: Designing all channels for one event
body:
Define every channel for an event at once, rather than adding each channel separately as it occurs to someone. Channels designed independently arrive at different times and describe different intensities.

Write the matrix before implementing: for each grade of the event, the visual response, the audio layer, the tactile pattern, and the time manipulation. Then implement it as one call site so an intensity change moves all four together.

Two failure modes come from doing this late. The first is drift - the visual is upgraded for a heavy hit while the audio stays at the light-hit clip, so the hit reads inconsistent. The second is stacking - each channel is individually reasonable, but together they exceed what the player can process, and the event becomes less readable than it was with two channels.

Accessibility falls out of the same matrix. Because the event is described in four channels, disabling one for comfort - motion, flash, vibration, or sound - still leaves the event fully legible. An event that exists in only one channel cannot be made accessible after the fact.

title: Choice symmetry
body:
Feedback should support a decision rather than steer it. Every path a player can take - proceed, hold, decline, close - must be equally findable, visually and spatially.

- Decline and later are default options, not exceptions. Give them the same visibility, size, and contrast as accept.
- Ease both sides equally. Animating only the accept button, or pulsing it alone, is asymmetry expressed as motion.
- Give each button its own clean feedback tone, so choosing the quiet option still feels like an action.
- Balance reconfirmation. Spending a significant asset deserves a confirmation step; declining does not. Requiring extra confirmation only to say no is pressure wearing the costume of safety.
- Default focus should sit on the safe option, not on the expensive one.

Worked example. On a failed attempt, place "Revive now (costs currency)" and "Return and resupply" at the same size and weight. Write the second as "Resupply and try again - your inventory is intact", not as a warning. The functional outcome is unchanged; what changes is whether the player trusts the screen the next time.

Popups and badges also need a cooldown structure: an offer declined once is not shown again immediately, "do not show again" works completely, and notification cadence is configurable.

Checklist:
- [ ] Are proceed, hold, later, and close equally clear?
- [ ] Does declining avoid extra confirmation steps that accepting does not require?
- [ ] Are cost, probability, and conditions readable before the choice, not after?
- [ ] Do cooldown and "do not show again" actually work?
- [ ] Are colour, size, and contrast balanced across all buttons?
- [ ] Does the default focus protect the player rather than the conversion?

title: Attention states and UI strategy
body:
The player is not in one mental state throughout. UI that suits focused execution is wrong for relaxed exploration, and the switch between them is itself a design surface.

| State | Player is | UI strategy |
|---|---|---|
| Focused execution | reacting, aiming, timing, deciding under pressure | key information immediate and close to the action, latency minimised, noise removed |
| Relaxed exploration | wandering, imagining, appreciating, planning | minimal UI, contextual information, soft transitions |
| Switching | detecting that something now matters | unmistakable signals for danger, reward, and new goals |

Rules per state. In focused execution keep the response inside 100ms, place critical values where the eye already is - near the character or at the edge nearest the action - and hold simultaneous elements to around seven. In relaxed exploration let content own 80% or more of the screen and show elements contextually, fading in and out over 0.2-0.3s.

Switching is where most UI damage happens. Announce a state change before it lands - audio cue before the enemy appears, a light change before the threat - and give a 2-3 second buffer coming out of intensity: result, then reward, then control returns. An unannounced switch is startle, not tension.

| Game shape | Balance | UI approach |
|---|---|---|
| Hardcore action | mostly focused | dense but strictly ordered combat information, immediate feedback |
| Balanced RPG | even | full UI in combat, minimal while exploring |
| Cosy or exploration | mostly relaxed | minimal, contextual, soft, no strong shake |
| Mobile live game | mixed | core values always visible, secondary information collapsible |

title: Cognitive load and screen budget
body:
Working memory is limited, and UI decides how much of it is spent on the interface instead of the game.

| Load | Meaning | Response |
|---|---|---|
| Intrinsic | complexity inherent to the task | manage with difficulty and teaching order, not with UI |
| Extraneous | burden added by the presentation | remove it; this is the only kind that is pure waste |
| Germane | burden that supports learning | strengthen it with feedback that explains what worked |

Screen budget. Keep UI under about 30% of the view. Past 40%, extraneous load rises sharply and fatigue arrives early. Strategy and simulation games can exceed it when the information is genuinely needed, but only with a much stronger hierarchy. Mobile layouts may need more area to satisfy touch targets, which is what collapsible and tabbed structures are for.

Hold simultaneous core elements to around seven. Beyond that the player stops reading the screen and starts scanning it, which is slower and less accurate.

Unity check. Measure rather than estimate: capture the game view and compare the UI area against the total, and count the elements a new player must read in the first ten seconds. Both numbers are usually higher than the team expects, because each element was added while the rest of the screen was ignored.

title: Visual hierarchy and the job of motion
body:
Hierarchy decides what is seen first, what reads as important, and in what order decisions are made. A screen is readable before it is beautiful.

Rank by consequence, then reinforce that rank with every available channel at once - position, size, contrast, and motion. When those four disagree, the player follows motion and contrast, so an unimportant element that pulses will beat a critical one that does not.

Motion has to answer at least one question: what changed, where did it come from and go to, what matters now, did that action succeed, where should attention go next. Motion that answers none of them is decoration and should be deleted; it costs attention that the important elements need.

Attention markers are a currency with a fixed supply. Badges, dots, pulses, and glows work only while they are scarce. A screen where several elements demand attention has no hierarchy at all, and the usual cause is that each marker was added by a different feature owner.

Practical pass for an existing screen: capture it, list every element that moves or glows, and cut until only the elements that change consequence remain. Then check the reading order by asking what a new player looks at first, second, and third, and whether that matches the order in which the screen expects decisions.

Hierarchy checklist:
- [ ] Is the most important information seen first?
- [ ] Do colour, size, position, and motion reinforce the same ranking?
- [ ] Are badges, dots, pulses, and glows scarce enough to still mean something?
- [ ] Does UI coverage leave the play view readable?
- [ ] Does every motion explain a state change or a location?
- [ ] Do strong visual effects sit behind accessibility options?
- [ ] Does readability outrank styling everywhere they conflict?

title: Diegetic UI
body:
Diegetic UI places information inside the world instead of overlaying it: state carried on the character, in the equipment, or in the environment rather than on a HUD panel.

It preserves immersion, reduces HUD area, and suits relaxed exploration especially well, because it removes the constant reminder that a system is being operated.

It fails in exactly one way: urgent information becomes hard to read. Health expressed as a subtle world cue is elegant while the player is comfortable and useless during the fight where it matters. The workable pattern is a hybrid - diegetic while calm, escalating to a direct and unmissable presentation when the value becomes critical.

Applications: state shown on the avatar itself through colour, aura, posture, or damage; objectives carried by world objects rather than a list; ammunition and charge readable on the equipment; and floating world-space labels near the object they describe instead of screen-space panels.

In Unity these live on a world-space Canvas or on renderers and materials rather than on the overlay Canvas. Two caveats: world-space UI needs a legibility check at the actual play distance and camera angle rather than in the editor viewport, and it must still respect the same contrast and text-size rules as screen-space UI.

title: Current visual styles and their costs
body:
Style choices carry mechanical costs. Adopt them for a reason and check the cost on the lowest-spec target.

Adaptive interfaces. Density and guidance adjust to skill, context, and fatigue: more guidance for beginners, less noise for experts, only combat elements during combat. The constraint is that adaptation is a copilot, never an autopilot - it must never override an explicit player setting, and its changes must be explainable, or the player loses the ability to predict their own interface.

Translucent panels and blur. Semi-transparent panels with a blurred background soften the boundary between world and interface. Keep background opacity at 60-80%, blur radius near 10px on handheld and 20px on desktop, borders at 1px with 20-30% white, and text contrast at 4.5:1 or better. Blur is a real per-pixel cost; on low-end hardware substitute a static blurred texture or a plain translucent panel, which reads almost identically in motion.

Soft tactile styling. Low-contrast raised surfaces look pleasant and hide button boundaries. Use it as an accent on key touchpoints only, mix it with flat elements, and never let it be the only signal that something is interactive.

Outcome-oriented structure. Organise around what the player is trying to achieve rather than around the screens the system happens to contain: what to do next rather than a raw quest list, relevant options rather than an entire catalogue, and settings routed by symptom - lag, motion discomfort, unreadable text - rather than by internal category.

title: Accessibility baseline
body:
Accessibility is baseline quality, not an optional feature, and most of it is cheap when planned and expensive when retrofitted.

| Area | Requirement |
|---|---|
| Colour | never carry information by colour alone; pair with icon, shape, or pattern |
| Contrast | text at 4.5:1 or better against its actual background |
| Text | adjustable UI text size, and layouts that survive the largest setting |
| Motion | separate reduction and off options for screen shake, camera motion, and strong transitions |
| Flashing | capped frequency and intensity, with a reduction option |
| Controls | full remapping, adequate touch targets, no required simultaneous inputs |
| Audio | captions for speech, visual alternatives for audio-only cues |
| Haptics | intensity and off options |

Design implication rather than a settings list: every event should be legible in more than one channel. If an event exists only as a flash, turning flashes off removes the event; if it also exists as a shape change and a sound, the same setting costs comfort and not information.

Unity notes. Reduced motion needs one multiplier that every motion system reads, so a single setting genuinely reaches all of it. Text size changes need layouts built to reflow rather than fixed rectangles. Test the largest text setting and the smallest supported resolution together - that combination is where fixed layouts break first.

title: Refining behavioural loops instead of discarding them
body:
Engagement design has real goals: return visits, repeated play, anticipation, growth, collection, event participation, conversion, retention. This category does not abandon those goals. It changes the path taken to reach them.

The single operating rule: preserve the functional outcome, but replace the mechanism. Deception, coercion, and opacity get swapped for immersion, convenience, rhythm, anticipation, achievement, and trust.

| Mechanism to retire | Mechanism that replaces it |
|---|---|
| Pressure | Invitation |
| Fear of loss | Preservation of value |
| Concealment | Transparency |
| Forced routine | A short, satisfying ritual |
| Cognitive fatigue | Support for faster judgement |
| Purchase pressure | A clear value proposition |
| Social guilt | Warm belonging |

The same substitution, written per system goal:

| Functional goal | Mechanism to retire | Mechanism that replaces it |
|---|---|---|
| Return visits | forced daily login | a short, satisfying return ritual |
| Event participation | "miss out and lose" framing | a pleasant bonus for taking part |
| Churn reduction | loss-avoidance pressure | continuity and preserved value |
| Conversion | purchase pressure | a clear value proposition |
| Repeated play | a compulsion loop | a rhythm of anticipation and achievement |
| Limited-time participation | manufactured scarcity | a seasonal world event with rerun information |
| Session pacing | stamina pressure | deliberate play-tempo regulation |
| Economy readability | a maze of convertible currencies | purpose-specific currencies with visible rates |
| Long-term retention | mechanisms that raise the cost of leaving | lowering the cost of returning |
| Social return | guilt-driven prompts | a warm invitation |

The distinction that matters is not how strong the feedback is, but what it amplifies. Good design amplifies actions that already carry meaning - a decision made, a skill applied, a goal reached. Bad design manufactures discomfort, scarcity, or anxiety and then uses presentation to make that pressure feel like fun.

At its strongest, feel becomes ownership: the player is not receiving feedback, they are expressing style and identifying with the result. Engagement built on that survives longer than engagement built on fear of losing progress, because it does not have to keep raising the stakes.

title: The seven-step loop and its two forms
body:
Manipulative and healthy loops share the same skeleton. The difference is what each step amplifies. Diagnose a system by walking the steps and asking which column it is standing in.

| Step | Risky form | Refined form |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Investment forms | progress that punishes absence | progress that helps a returning player recover context |
| 2. Loss is signalled | "you will lose this if you stop" | plain information about remaining opportunities |
| 3. Anticipation builds | near-miss framing, inflated perceived odds | tension proportional to actual outcome value |
| 4. Friction is placed | artificial inconvenience and stalls | hurdles that teach strategy and mastery |
| 5. A resolution path is emphasised | the paid path is brightest and easiest | multiple paths presented for comparison |
| 6. Juice justifies it | removing system friction is celebrated as achievement | actual choice and achievement are celebrated |
| 7. The routine normalises | obligation and fatigue become the habit | a short, pleasant return ritual |

Rules operate at three scales, and each has its own failure.

| Scale | What it governs | Failure |
|---|---|---|
| High-level | long-term goals, progression gates, return reasons, economy shape | rest, absence, or non-payment costs identity or core progress |
| Mid-level | the meaning of objects, offers, events, deadlines, rewards | one option is made to feel mandatory through urgency or asymmetry |
| Low-level | durability, reward value, damage, cost, cooldown, exchange rates | weak value hidden behind strong presentation or unclear rates |

Because rules manufacture value that has no meaning outside the system, they carry a higher transparency burden than anything else in the design. A currency, a drop rate, or an unlock condition is only as fair as it is legible before the commitment.

title: Investment without punishment for resting
body:
Investment is powerful: time, effort, emotion, currency, and social identity all deepen attachment. The failure begins when investment turns into something the player loses by resting.

Principles.
- Use accumulated progress to show the player their own history, not their exposure to loss.
- Treat a break as a pause, never as decay.
- Help returning players recover context fast - what they were doing, what changed, what is next.
- Keep streaks as a bonus. The moment a streak governs core growth, the game has made attendance mandatory.
- Provide grace days, recovery tickets, or alternative routes for missed rewards.

Say: "Your progress is saved. Continue whenever you are ready."
Do not say: "If you leave now, today's reward disappears."

Both sentences describe the same system state. The first leaves the player free to stop; the second spends trust to buy one more session, and it has to be spent again tomorrow.

Diagnostic: if a player rests for a week, does the design lose them a bonus, or does it lose them standing? A bonus is acceptable. Standing is not.

title: Uncertainty that stays honest
body:
Uncertain rewards are legitimate and often excellent: exploration, drops, run variation, reveals, and chests all use uncertainty well. The failure begins when failure is dressed as near-success, or when presentation makes a reward look more likely or more valuable than it is.

Principles.
- Disclose probability, duplicate handling, pity systems, and consolation value plainly, before the commitment.
- Match reveal intensity to actual value. A long dramatic build that resolves into a common item teaches the player that the build means nothing.
- Represent failure honestly while granting real accumulated value - a visible pity gauge that actually advances.
- Use near-miss framing rarely and carefully; manufacturing it is the clearest line between tension and manipulation.
- Do not make immediate retry the only large, obvious action on the result screen.

A result sequence that holds up: reveal the result, show the actual reward, advance the milestone gauge visibly, then offer inventory, preparation, and retry as comparable options.

The measurable version of this: if the presentation were removed, would the player value the reward the same way? If not, the presentation is doing the work the reward should be doing.

title: Friction that asks for judgement
body:
Friction is not the problem. Without it there is no challenge and no achievement. The question is what the friction asks for: judgement, skill, strategy, and planning are legitimate; tolerance for tedium is not.

A strategic hurdle changes how the player values their actions. It should focus attention on better play, on build choice, or on revealing mastery. If a rule only changes how much discomfort the player will endure, it is not a hurdle, it is a toll.

Principles.
