- A hurdle should teach something. If clearing it produces no new understanding, it is padding.
- The free path must remain real play, not unpaid labour with the fun removed.
- Paid options should save time or expand choice - never remove pain that was manufactured to be sold back.
- The cause of the hurdle must be understandable, so the player can respond with a strategy instead of a wallet.
- Celebration after clearing it must attach to the player's decision or skill.

Reward rules should name the verbs the game wants to make valuable. If the design wants risk-taking, precision, exploration, chain play, or recovery, the rewards have to reinforce those specific behaviours - a reward net wide enough to welcome everything teaches nothing about what is worth mastering.

Diagnostics: does this hurdle make the player better; is the free path enjoyable or merely long; is the paid option a preference or effectively mandatory?

title: Belonging without obligation
body:
Cooperative systems are among the strongest reasons players return, and among the easiest to convert into obligation without noticing, because the pressure comes from other players rather than from the design.

Principles.
- One member's rest must not directly damage the group's outcome. Build the buffer into the system so the group never has to police attendance.
- Never expose absence publicly. Ranked contribution boards that show who did not participate turn a social feature into an attendance register.
- Provide alternative contribution paths - donation, asynchronous help, banked contribution - so that participation survives an irregular schedule.
- Make notifications invitations. "A new event opened, join when you are free" and "your team is waiting for you" describe the same event and produce different relationships.
- Support returning players deliberately: catch-up mechanisms, a summary of what changed, and a welcome rather than a penalty.

Diagnostic: if a player takes a week off, does the group lose points or does the player lose standing among people they know? The second is the one that turns a game into an obligation, and it is very hard to reverse once the group has learned to expect attendance.

title: Interfaces that support judgement
body:
The best interface for a decision is one where the player can act exactly as they intend without fatigue, at their own pace.

Principles.
- Control exposure frequency of popups, badges, and confirmation windows. Each one spends attention the player cannot recover.
- Lay out proceed, hold, and close with equal visual weight.
- Treat decline and defer as normal options, not as failure states.
- Give the player enough information, and enough time, to judge before asking for a decision.
- Record and honour the decision that was made, including the negative one.

Worked example. A continue-or-return prompt after a failed attempt places "Revive now (costs currency)" and "Return and resupply" at equal size and contrast. Choosing to return is answered with "Resupply and try again - your inventory is intact", not with a warning. Choosing to revive is answered with a fast, clean return to play. Both paths get a real response.

Fatigue is a design surface. A decision asked at the end of a long session, on a screen with a countdown, from a player who has already made twenty decisions, is not the same decision asked at the start. Designs that consistently place their most expensive prompts at the point of highest fatigue are choosing where the player is weakest.

title: Presentation that matches real value
body:
Presentation intensity is a claim about importance. When the claim is wrong, the player either misreads the game or stops trusting the presentation, and both are expensive.

| Presentation | Correct use | What it buys |
|---|---|---|
| Full burst and fanfare | a genuinely hard clear or a long-term goal completed | catharsis that lands because it was earned |
| Tier colour | the item's actual rarity and value | the tier vocabulary keeps predicting value |
| Countdown or timer | a real deadline, stated accurately | the player can plan around it |
| Attention badge | new content or something the player asked to be told about | the badge keeps meaning something |
| Pulsing highlight | the one action that is genuinely next | reduced confusion instead of added noise |

Audio honesty. Sound is the fastest channel for interpreting an outcome, so a triumphant line over a poor result is the most efficient way to teach a player not to trust the audio. Match the tone to the actual result, mix the pre-reveal build against the real value range, and keep timers calm rather than anxious.

Motion honesty. Ease both sides of a choice equally, put the default focus on the safe option, and provide a skip for result presentation - a celebration the player cannot skip stops being a reward on the second viewing.

Deadline guidance, structurally. A real deadline is information; the structure around it decides whether it stays information.

Workable: "This seasonal reward ends in 3 days." with Join now / View later / Set reminder as equal options.
Not workable: "If you quit now, you will lose this limited reward forever." with Continue / Give up benefits as the only paths.

Both describe the same deadline. The first supports planning; the second converts the same fact into pressure and labels the decline path as a loss.

title: Wording
body:
Wording is where an otherwise fair system reveals what it is optimising for. The same state can be described as information or as a threat.

- State the value plainly: "Selecting this returns you to the resupply area. Your buffs are preserved."
- Invite rather than summon: "A new raid is open. Join when you are ready."
- Preserve agency: "This is a seasonal offer. You can find it again in the shop at any time."
- Frame growth rather than loss: "A new opportunity to grow" rather than "Do not miss out."
- Keep option labels neutral: "Check later" and "Start now", never "Give up rewards" and "Continue".

The last one matters most. Labelling the decline option as a loss - "give up", "abandon", "lose your bonus" - is the cheapest manipulation available and the easiest to spot, because the label describes a consequence the system invented for the purpose of labelling it.

Write the negative path first. If the decline label cannot be written without implying failure, the underlying system is the problem, not the copy.

title: Disclosure before commitment
body:
Everything the player needs to judge must be on screen before the decision, not reachable afterwards.

- Price, probability, conditions of use, expiry, and refund rules appear at the point of choice.
- Probability-based content carries a one-touch route to the full odds, including pity thresholds and duplicate conversion.
- Free and paid routes are laid out so their time and currency costs can be compared directly, without arithmetic the player has to perform.
- Exchange rates between currencies are visible wherever the exchange happens.
- Nothing material lives only in a patch note or an external page.

The test is timing, not availability. Disclosure that exists but arrives after the commitment is the same as no disclosure. Multiple currency layers deserve specific attention here, because each conversion step is a place where the real price becomes harder to compute - and a price the player cannot compute is not a price they agreed to.

title: Four common systems, refined
body:
The recurring systems in live games each have a well-known manipulative form and a well-known workable one. The functional goal is identical in both.

Check-in and attendance. Goal: return visits and a small welcome. Missing one day must not damage core progress; streak rewards stay bonuses; grace days, recovery tickets, or comeback rewards exist; the ritual reads as a greeting rather than a duty.

Reward reveal and boxes. Goal: anticipation and a strong reward moment. Probability, pity, and duplicate value are disclosed; reveal intensity matches actual value; a miss still advances real accumulated value; the result screen offers inventory and preparation alongside retry rather than making retry the only obvious action.

Growth hurdles and boosters. Goal: turn a plateau into a decision. The hurdle requires new learning or experimentation; the free path stays enjoyable; boosters save time or expand choice; the celebration credits the player's judgement rather than the purchase.

Ranking and competition. Goal: comparison that produces growth rather than anxiety. Show personal best and improvement over time alongside rank; avoid emphasising rank loss on its own; keep competition as feedback rather than as a standing that must be defended daily.

Across all four, the same question separates the two forms: if the presentation and the urgency were removed, would the player still want this? If yes, the presentation is amplifying. If no, it is substituting.

title: Signal-level replacements
body:
A table of the concrete substitutions, for reviewing an existing system without redesigning it.

| Area | Target signal | Mechanism that delivers it |
|---|---|---|
| Attendance | absence does not damage accumulated progress | grace days, return rewards, in-play recovery routes |
| Reward reveal | presentation matches real value | odds and pity always visible, milestone accrual per attempt |
| Content options | several routes suited to the player's situation | choices across time, convenience, and play style |
| Prompts and popups | accept, hold, and close are equally clear | cooldown after a decline, a complete "do not show again" |
| Notifications | information and invitation only | configurable cadence, welcome rather than summons |
| Ranking | growth measured against the player's own history | personal best and improvement shown beside rank |
| Guild and community | one absence does not damage the group | automatic buffering, alternative contribution |
| Audio | tone matches the real outcome | honest result tone, feedback preserved even on skip |
| Motion | emphasis follows real importance | no pulsing that favours one option over another |

Used as a review pass, this table converts "this system feels manipulative" into a specific list of mechanisms to change, which is the form the objection has to take before it can be acted on.

title: Testing behavioural changes safely
body:
When testing engagement patterns with real players, the test must not create real loss.

- No real payment, no real account loss, no loss of real rare resources.
- Informed consent before the session, and a debrief after it that explains what the layout was testing.
- A visible, always-available stop.
- Compare the pressured variant and the refined variant side by side rather than testing the pressured one alone.
- Anonymise the data.
- The purpose is to understand the mechanism and validate a safe alternative, not to find the maximum tolerable pressure.

The evaluation criterion matters as much as the safety rules. A test that optimises only for a metric will always select the more pressured variant, because pressure moves metrics first and costs trust later, outside the measurement window. Judge on the balance between voluntary engagement and comfort, and measure retention over a period long enough for the cost to appear.

title: The line
body:
Behavioural design is legitimate. These specific mechanisms are not: deception, opacity, unrecoverable loss, coercive pressure, and exploitation of cognitive fatigue.

| Area | Acceptable | Not acceptable |
|---|---|---|
| Limited-time content | accurate duration and rerun information | manufactured "never again" pressure |
| Rewards | visible probability, pity, duplicate value | hidden odds, exaggerated near-miss effects |
| Purchases | time saved, cosmetics, expanded choice | the only remedy for manufactured discomfort |
| Popups | useful guidance with frequency limits | repeated interruption, obstructed refusal |
| Notifications | information and invitation | guilt, fear of loss |
| Social systems | cooperation and welcome | public pressure, shaming absence |
| Presentation | amplifying achievement | disguising pressure as achievement |
| Rules | clear costs, gates, and consequences | hidden exchange rates, opaque loss |

Five principles.
1. Information comes before the decision - price, odds, conditions, duration, and cancellation.
2. Every choice is findable. Decline, later, close, and settings are not hidden.
3. Stopping is not failure. Resting, exiting, and postponing are respected paths.
4. Presentation matches real value. Over-presenting weak outcomes buys clicks today and costs trust permanently.
5. Engagement must not spend trust. Good engagement makes the player want to return tomorrow; bad engagement makes them press something today.

Final questions. Does the player act because they want to, or because not acting feels costly? Does this interface help judgement, or fatigue the player toward one button? Does this presentation amplify achievement, or amplify manufactured anxiety? Can the player stop and still feel their time was respected?

title: Engagement and ethics checklist
body:
System and progression:
- [ ] Is core progress preserved when the player rests and returns?
- [ ] Do long-term systems avoid making daily attendance a requirement for core growth?
- [ ] Do hurdles ask for strategy or mastery rather than tolerance?
- [ ] Do paid options expand choice or save time, rather than removing manufactured pain?
- [ ] Is reward presentation proportional to actual value?

Choice structure:
- [ ] Are proceed, hold, later, and close equally clear?
- [ ] Does declining avoid extra confirmation that accepting does not require?
- [ ] Are cost, probability, and conditions readable before the choice?
- [ ] Do cooldown and "do not show again" work completely?
- [ ] Are colour, size, and contrast balanced across all options?

Presentation honesty:
- [ ] Does celebration match the scale of what was actually achieved?
- [ ] Is a poor result presented honestly rather than dressed up?
- [ ] Does the audio match the real meaning of the event?
- [ ] Can result presentation be skipped on repeat viewings?
- [ ] Do motion and timing serve comfort and comprehension first?

Community:
- [ ] Does the group system avoid penalising an individual's rest?
- [ ] Is non-participation handled without public exposure?
- [ ] Do limited rewards have a rerun or an alternative route?
- [ ] Does competition encourage personal growth rather than daily defence?
- [ ] Is every notification useful information or a genuine invitation?

Final:
- [ ] Would the player still want this if the urgency and the presentation were removed?

title: Anti-patterns
body:
Named failures, with the fix that actually addresses each cause rather than its symptom.

| Anti-pattern | Symptom | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| Silent interaction | the player repeats an input, unsure it registered | every interactive element gets at least a visual change and a sound |
| Effect cover-up | effects are added to hide an action that is not interesting | strengthen the action's meaning first; amplification cannot create it |
| Over-shake | everything shakes, nothing reads as impact | cap shake by event grade and clamp the total |
| Inconsistent weight | a small action gets a large response, or visual and audio disagree | match the weight of the feedback to the weight of the action, and align timing within about 50ms |
| Metaphor mismatch | visuals promise one physical reality, motion and collision deliver another | change the treatment, or tune the response to match the promise |
| Abrupt transition | the screen cuts with no fade, the mode changes with no warning | animate every transition, pre-announce mode changes, buffer the exit from intensity |
| UI fireworks | menus bounce and pulse constantly | reserve emphasis for the core interaction points |
| Fake urgency | everything looks urgent, so nothing is | use urgency only for real deadlines and real importance |
| Reward inflation | ordinary results are presented as legendary | match presentation to actual value |
| Popup siege | prompts surround the player | frequency limits, a queue, cooldown after a decline |
| Hidden decline | refusing is hard to find or requires extra steps | place all choices symmetrically |
| Motion sickness | camera and shake overuse | intensity sliders and a reduced-motion mode |
| Cognitive fog | too much information to decide with | hierarchy and progressive disclosure |
| Mobile transplant | a desktop layout shipped to a touchscreen | 44x44pt targets, shake at 70-80%, collapsible structures, safe-area respect |

One failure sits behind several of the others: losing objectivity about a build you have played for months. Adaptation is silent and monotonic - shake intensity that reads as correct after a year of exposure is often nauseating on first contact, and a control scheme that feels obvious to its author is frequently unreadable to a new player. Watch new players play without narrating, and treat feel values as the settings most in need of outside calibration.

title: Match intensity to what the screen asks
body:
One principle threads through the anti-patterns: the strength of the presentation should be proportional to what the screen is for.

- Reward and celebration screens - level up, results, victory - can carry exaggeration freely. Here it is the point.
- Precision screens - forms, drag interactions, text entry, competitive HUDs - stay calm. Strong motion costs accuracy and readability, and accuracy is what the screen is for.
- Anything strong sits behind a reduced-motion or intensity option.

The consequence is that the same effect can be correct on one screen and wrong on the next, so an effect library cannot be applied uniformly. Ask what this screen asks the player to do, then set intensity from the answer.

The corollary is about restraint in the right place. Removing motion from a celebration screen makes an earned moment feel unacknowledged. Adding it to an input-heavy screen makes an ordinary task harder. Both are the same mistake - intensity chosen by taste rather than by function.

title: Presentation must match real value
body:
Where the previous principle scales intensity to the screen's purpose, this one scales it to the value of what the player actually accomplished. It is the difference between amplification and misrepresentation.

- Reserve the strongest visual vocabulary for genuinely difficult clears and long-term goals. When visual intensity exceeds real importance, the player misreads the game and then stops trusting the signal.
- Match tier colour and effect to actual rarity, so the vocabulary keeps predicting value.
- Mix the pre-reveal build against the real range of outcomes. A build that promises more than the distribution can deliver produces disappointment on every average result.
- Present a poor outcome honestly, and show the real accumulated value instead - a pity gauge that visibly advances is honest; a triumphant fanfare over a common item is not.
- Attach celebration to the player's decision. Feedback that supports a cautious choice - retreating, resupplying, saving a resource - is part of this, because a game that only celebrates spending has told the player what it values.

The quality question for any celebration: does this amplify the joy of something the player actually earned, or does it manufacture a feeling the outcome did not deserve?

title: Baseline checklist, all games
body:
Input and response:
- [ ] Do core inputs produce a visible response within 100ms?
- [ ] Do acceleration and deceleration match each object's identity and mass?
- [ ] Are lock-out and cancel rules readable before the player commits?
- [ ] Do buffers and grace windows remove unfair failure without being visible?
- [ ] Does the same input reliably produce the same result, independent of frame rate?
- [ ] After a failure, can the player tell whether the cause was their decision or the system?

Interface:
- [ ] Does every button have a press and a release response, plus a sound?
- [ ] Are disabled states clearly distinguished, with a reason where the block is not obvious?
- [ ] Does every screen transition have an animation?
- [ ] Do numbers and bars make the size of a change felt, not just readable?
- [ ] Are decline and defer laid out as normal options?

Amplification:
- [ ] Is there an intensity grade per event, applied consistently?
- [ ] Do visual, audio, tactile, and time responses describe the same event within about 50ms?
- [ ] Can the presentation be removed without changing the rules or the simulation?
- [ ] Are low-value outcomes left un-inflated?

Accessibility:
- [ ] Is there a shake and camera-motion intensity setting, with a genuine off?
- [ ] Is information carried by something other than colour alone?
- [ ] Is UI text size adjustable, and does the layout survive the largest setting?
- [ ] Does every audio cue have a visual counterpart?
- [ ] Is flashing capped in frequency and intensity, with a reduction option?

Session:
- [ ] Is the first goal visible within the first 30 seconds?
- [ ] Can a short session still feel complete?
- [ ] After failure, is there a clear recovery path?
- [ ] After a reward, does the next goal appear naturally?
- [ ] Does the session end leave satisfaction rather than pressure?

title: Additional checklist, action and combat
body:
- [ ] Is there hit stop, graded by hit strength and capped when hits repeat?
- [ ] Is there knockback, scaled by target mass rather than applied as a constant?
- [ ] Do hits produce a visible reaction on the target itself - flash, flinch, deformation?
- [ ] Is there a camera reaction on impact, applied as an offset rather than written into the follow target?
- [ ] Do defeated enemies leave something behind, even briefly?
- [ ] Is there enough particle response, directed against the contact rather than radially?
- [ ] Do chains and combos have escalating feedback, with the audio ladder distinct from pitch randomisation?
- [ ] Is input buffered across hit stop, recovery, and animation lock-out?
- [ ] Is the control-loss budget on player knockback capped and consistent?
- [ ] Is the multi-channel matrix defined per hit grade, rather than per channel?

title: Additional checklist, cosy and exploration
body:
- [ ] Is the UI minimal, appearing contextually rather than permanently?
- [ ] Are transitions unhurried, with nothing that startles?
- [ ] Is feedback soft - no strong shake, no aggressive flashing?
- [ ] Is repeated audio pleasant across a long session, with pitch variation on repeats?
- [ ] Is there nothing that rushes the player - no countdowns on ordinary actions, no urgency badges by default?
- [ ] Does the game read well while the player is relaxed and only half-attending?
- [ ] Are ambient systems bounded so a long session does not accumulate clutter or cost?
- [ ] Can the session end at any moment without losing meaningful progress?

title: Additional checklist, strategy and simulation
body:
- [ ] Is the higher information density justified by decisions the player actually makes?
- [ ] Is there a strict visual hierarchy, so density does not become noise?
- [ ] Does state change carry a visible response, even when nothing moves in the world?
- [ ] Is progressive disclosure used, so depth is reachable without being permanently on screen?
- [ ] Are numbers animated enough to show a change occurred, without slowing rapid interaction?
- [ ] Is feedback on repeated bulk actions kept light, so it survives hundreds of repetitions?
- [ ] Can the player tell which of several simultaneous changes was caused by their last action?
- [ ] Are alerts ranked, so an important event is distinguishable from routine ones?

title: Additional checklist, mobile
body:
- [ ] Are touch targets at least 44x44pt or 48x48dp, expanding the raycast area rather than the artwork?
- [ ] Is there immediate press feedback, given that there is no hover state?
- [ ] Is haptic feedback applied to core interactions, with an off option?
- [ ] Is shake reduced to 70-80%, since the same displacement is a larger fraction of a small screen?
- [ ] Are particles and effects bounded for battery and thermal cost?
- [ ] Does the layout respect the safe area on notched and gesture-bar devices?
- [ ] Does the UI scale across aspect ratios, including foldables and tablets?
- [ ] Are blur and other per-pixel effects substituted on low-end hardware?
- [ ] Are destructive actions spaced away from routine ones to prevent mis-taps?
- [ ] Is one-handed reach considered for the most frequent action?

title: Production workflow for a feel or engagement system
body:
A sequence that keeps feel work from becoming an open-ended polish pass.

1. Define the intent. What emotion and what behaviour should this produce? One sentence, before any values.
2. Identify the player action. What must they press, see, understand, and remember?
3. Map the layers. Which of core feel, UI feel, juice, session arc, and engagement are actually involved?
4. Set the intensity grade. Match the presentation grade to the event's real value before building it.
5. Check the ethical boundary. Are information, choices, rest, and reward value transparent?
6. Prototype the smallest loop. Input, response, reward - nothing else - and judge it in play, not in the inspector.
7. Playtest. Watch behaviour rather than collecting opinions; the useful signal is where players hesitate, repeat an input, or misread a state.
8. Check fatigue. Does it survive the hundredth repetition, or only the first?
9. Check accessibility. Are there alternatives for motion, colour, sound, and haptics?
10. Record the values. Numbers, curves, audio, haptics, and exceptions, so the tuning survives the person who did it.

Order of construction, when building the supporting systems in a Unity project. First the foundations: a tweening or curve utility, an audio manager with pooling and mixer routing, and one reusable button component covering all five states. Then the core response systems: pooled particle presets, a shake system with grade and decay and a global intensity multiplier, a hit-stop system with unscaled UI and input buffering, and event-to-sound mapping with pitch variation. Then the detail layer: character personality, ambient systems, camera look-ahead and kick, haptics, and persistence of remains with pooling.

Build the accessibility multipliers into the core systems in the second step, not as a later pass. Retrofitting one global intensity value into a dozen systems that each read their own is where the option quietly stops covering everything.

title: Making feel toggleable and testable
body:
Do not treat feel as one property. Split it into independently toggleable elements, so their contribution can be judged one at a time and their absence can be tested.

| Category | Examples | Verification question |
|---|---|---|
| Impact feedback | hit flash, sparks, brief freeze | does the collision read instantly? |
| Camera response | shake, kick, zoom, dead zone | does it convey force without stealing the view? |
| Elasticity | squash and stretch, landing compression, dash stretch | does the body's weight match input and motion? |
| Physical reaction | knockback, impulses, remains and debris | does the action change the space? |
| Input forgiveness | buffers, coyote time, step assist, ledge assist | does it remove unfair failure? |
| Trails | projectile trails, dust, shells, afterimages | can the player read path and consequence? |
| Time modulation | hit stop, slow motion, ramping | does it make important moments easier to perceive? |

Each toggle needs three pieces of metadata, not just a boolean: a name that identifies the element, a description of the sensation it is supposed to produce, and the trigger condition that says when to look for it. With those, the options list becomes an instrument for comparison instead of a list of switches.

Acceptance checklist before adding a new feel element:
- [ ] Can it be toggled independently of everything else?
- [ ] Is its trigger condition explicit?
- [ ] Is its intensity value or grade recorded?
- [ ] Do the rules and progression still work with it disabled?
- [ ] Is a reduced-motion variant possible?
- [ ] Does it match the object's representation and treatment?
- [ ] Is it still pleasant on the hundredth repetition?
- [ ] Does it avoid duplicating an existing effect into noise?
- [ ] Does it make the player's action easier to read?

The reason this matters beyond tuning: if presentation cannot be disabled without breaking the rules, then presentation has quietly become simulation, and the accessibility options that switch it off will break the game rather than soften it.
